topic: understanding the concept of the difference between permutations and combinations formulas

easy.text: The permutation formula P(n,r) = n!/(n-r)! is used when:

options.feedback: Correct -- permutations count arrangements where different orderings of the same items are considered distinct outcomes.

options.text: The order of selection does not matter at all
options.feedback: That describes when to use the COMBINATION formula, not the permutation formula, which specifically applies when order DOES matter.

options.text: You are selecting zero items from a group
options.feedback: This isn't the defining condition for using the permutation formula -- the key factor is whether ORDER matters, not the specific number of items selected.

options.text: The group being selected from is infinitely large
options.feedback: Group size (finite or otherwise) isn't the defining condition for using the permutation formula -- the key factor is whether order of selection matters.

medium.text: In how many ways can a President and a Vice President be selected from a group of 5 candidates (assuming no one can hold both positions)? Since these are distinct roles, use the permutation formula P(5,2)=5!/(5-2)!

options.feedback: This would be the result of the COMBINATION formula C(5,2), not the permutation formula, but since President/VP are distinct roles, order (who gets which role) matters here.
This is just the total number of candidates, not the correctly calculated number of ways to select two distinct role-holders.
This doesn't correctly result from applying the permutation formula calculation for this scenario.

hard.text: A committee of 3 people (with no distinct roles -- everyone is just a regular 'committee member') needs to be chosen from a group of 6 candidates. Explain why the COMBINATION formula C(6,3), rather than the permutation formula, is the correct approach here, and calculate the result.

options.text: Since committee membership doesn't involve distinct roles (order doesn't matter -- choosing person A, B, C creates the same committee as choosing C, B, A), the combination formula applies: C(6,3)=6!/(3!×3!)=20
options.feedback: Correct -- since there's no distinction between committee members' roles (unlike President vs. Vice President), the specific ORDER of selection doesn't create a different outcome, making combination (not permutation) the appropriate approach here.

options.text: The permutation formula would actually give the exact same correct answer as the combination formula here
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- the permutation formula P(6,3) would give 120 (a different, INCORRECT answer for this scenario), since it would incorrectly treat different orderings of the same 3 people as distinct outcomes, which doesn't apply here since committee membership has no distinct roles.

options.text: The combination formula happens to be simply irrelevant to this type of selection scenario
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- the combination formula is actually PRECISELY the correct, relevant tool for this specific type of scenario, since order doesn't matter for undifferentiated committee membership.

options.text: Order of selection actually DOES matter in this specific committee scenario, contrary to what's being suggested
options.feedback: This isn't accurate -- since all committee members hold the SAME undifferentiated role (no distinct positions like President/VP), order of selection specifically does NOT matter here, which is why combination (not permutation) is the correct approach.

easy.hard: This formula applies specifically when distinguishable ordering among the selected elements constitutes functionally different outcomes.
easy.medium: Use this formula when swapping the order of your selections would actually create a different, distinct result.
easy.easy: Use this when swapping the order of picks creates a different result.

medium.hard: Since the two positions are functionally distinct, apply the permutation formula directly using the given values for n and r.
medium.medium: Plug 5 and 2 into the permutation formula: 5! divided by (5-2)!.
medium.easy: Calculate 5×4=20 (since these are the two relevant terms in the permutation calculation).

hard.hard: Determine whether the selected group members hold functionally distinguishable roles (requiring permutation) or an undifferentiated collective role (requiring combination), then apply the appropriate formula.
hard.medium: Since all committee members are treated the same (no special roles), use the combination formula instead of the permutation formula.
hard.easy: Since committee members have no special roles, use combinations: C(6,3)=20.
